c: A switch worked by voltage

A MOSFET has three terminals: gate, drain and source. Current flows between drain and source, and the voltage on the gate decides whether that path is open or closed. The gate is separated from the rest of the device by a thin layer of glass-like oxide, so no steady current flows into it. A bipolar transistor needs base current for as long as it is on. A MOSFET needs only a voltage, held there like pressure on a button.
The threshold

An N-channel MOSFET begins to conduct when the gate is a few volts above the source. That starting point is the threshold voltage, and it is often misread. At the threshold the device is barely on. To turn it on fully, the gate needs to be well above that. Standard power MOSFETs want about 10 volts. Parts described as logic level are built to be fully on at 4.5 volts or even 2.5, which is what a microcontroller pin can supply.
On-resistance

When fully on, a MOSFET behaves like a very small resistor between drain and source. The datasheet gives this figure, the on-resistance, and for power parts it is measured in thousandths of an ohm. That is why MOSFETs dominate at high current. Ten amps through one hundredth of an ohm dissipates just one watt. A bipolar transistor carrying the same current would waste several watts and need a substantial heatsink to survive.
The basic low-side switch

The standard circuit puts the load between the positive supply and the drain, with the source connected to ground. Drive the gate high and the load turns on. Two small resistors complete it. One of about 100 ohms in series with the gate limits the brief rush of current as the gate charges. One of 10 kilohms or more from gate to ground holds the gate low when the controlling pin is not yet driving, so the load does not twitch on at power-up.
The gate is a capacitor

Although no steady current enters the gate, it has capacitance, and that capacitance must be charged and discharged each time the device switches. During the moment it is partly on, the MOSFET dissipates a lot of heat. Switch it once a second and this is irrelevant. Switch it tens of thousands of times a second, as in a motor controller, and it matters greatly. That is why fast circuits use a dedicated driver chip to push the gate up and down quickly.
N-channel and P-channel

N-channel MOSFETs turn on with the gate above the source and are used to switch the ground side of a load. P-channel devices turn on with the gate below the source and are used to switch the positive side. N-channel parts are cheaper and have lower resistance for their size, so designers use them wherever they can. Inside logic chips, the two types are paired so that one is always off, which is the arrangement known as CMOS.
Handle with a little care

The oxide under the gate is extremely thin, and a static discharge from your finger can punch through it. Most gates are rated for only about 20 volts either way. Modern parts have some protection, but it is sensible to touch something grounded before handling them and to keep them in their conductive packaging until needed. A MOSFET damaged by static may fail at once or may work for a while and then die without warning.
The built-in diode

Every power MOSFET contains a diode between source and drain as a by-product of how it is made. It points the opposite way to normal current flow. This means a MOSFET cannot block current in the reverse direction: connect the supply backwards and the diode conducts. Sometimes the diode is useful, carrying the kickback current from a motor. Either way, you need to know it is there. It appears on the schematic symbol as a small diode drawn across the transistor.
What the panel is

Electricity enters a house through one large cable and is divided at the panel into many separate circuits, each serving a few rooms or a single large appliance. Every circuit passes through its own breaker, a switch that turns itself off if too much current flows. At the top is a main breaker that cuts power to the whole house. In North America, typical homes have service of 100 to 200 amps. The panel is the one place where you can shut everything off.
Why breakers exist

Wire heats up as current passes through it, and a wire carrying more than it is rated for can get hot enough to start a fire inside a wall. Each breaker is matched to the wire it protects. A 15 amp breaker protects the thinner wire used for lighting and ordinary outlets. A 20 amp breaker protects the heavier wire used in kitchens and bathrooms. When the current exceeds the rating, the breaker trips before the wire overheats.
The arithmetic of an overload

In a 120 volt system, a 15 amp circuit can deliver 1,800 watts, and for loads that run for hours the safe figure is about 1,440. A portable heater draws about 1,500 watts by itself. A hair dryer draws nearly the same. Run two such appliances on one circuit and the breaker will trip, exactly as designed. The usual cause of a tripped breaker is not a fault. It is too many things plugged into the same circuit.
How to reset one

A tripped breaker sits in a middle position or has moved to off, and some show a coloured flag. Unplug or switch off what was running on that circuit. Push the breaker handle firmly all the way to off, then back to on. It should stay. If it trips again immediately with nothing connected, there is a fault in the wiring or the breaker, and that is a job for an electrician. Do not keep resetting it.
Ground fault protection

Some outlets and breakers have test and reset buttons. These are ground fault interrupters. They compare the current going out with the current coming back, and if a few thousandths of an amp go missing, perhaps through a person, they cut the power in a fraction of a second. They are required near water: kitchens, bathrooms, garages and outdoors. Press the test button every month or so. The power should cut off, and reset should restore it.
Arc fault protection

Newer homes also have arc fault breakers, which listen electronically for the signature of sparking in damaged wires or loose connections, a common cause of house fires. They can be tripped by some older appliances and tools. If one trips repeatedly on a particular device, the device may be at fault. If it trips for no evident reason, have the circuit checked. It may be detecting a genuine problem inside a wall.
Label the circuits

Many panels have a chart inside the door that is blank, wrong or illegible. An afternoon spent correcting it is well used. Turn off one breaker at a time and note what stops working, with a lamp or radio plugged in as an indicator. Write the result clearly. In an emergency, or when you simply want to change a light fitting safely, knowing which breaker controls what saves time and removes guesswork.
When to call a professional

Some signs should never be ignored: a breaker that feels hot, a burning or fishy smell near the panel or an outlet, buzzing or crackling, scorch marks, or lights that dim sharply when an appliance starts. Never replace a breaker with a larger one to stop it tripping, since that removes the protection for the wire. Resetting breakers and labelling circuits are tasks for a householder. Work inside the panel is for a licensed electrician.
What flow is

Flow is a state of complete absorption in an activity. Attention narrows to the task. Self-consciousness fades. Time seems to speed up or slow down. Action and awareness merge, so that you are doing the thing without watching yourself do it. The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, who studied it for decades beginning in the 1970s, found the same description from rock climbers, surgeons, chess players, musicians and factory workers. He chose the word because so many of them said it felt like being carried by a current.
The balance of challenge and skill

The central condition is a match between how hard the task is and how capable you are. If the challenge is far above your skill, you feel anxious. If it is far below, you feel bored. Flow occurs in the channel between, where the task stretches you without overwhelming you. Because skill grows with practice, the challenge must grow as well. This is why a game that was gripping at first becomes dull once you have mastered it.
Clear goals

The second condition is knowing, moment to moment, what you are trying to do. A climber's goal is the next hold. A musician's is the next phrase. Vague tasks such as work on the report resist flow, because part of your mind is occupied with deciding what to do next. Breaking a large project into a concrete next action, such as draft the three paragraphs of the findings section, supplies the clarity that absorption needs.
Immediate feedback

The third condition is that you can tell at once how you are doing. A tennis player sees where the ball lands. A programmer runs the code and it works or fails. Activities with slow or ambiguous feedback, such as management or long-term research, rarely produce flow unaided. You can sometimes build feedback in: a word count that rises, a checklist that shortens, a test that passes. The loop between action and result needs to be short.
No interruptions

Flow takes time to enter, commonly ten to twenty minutes of sustained attention, and a single interruption ends it. A notification, a question from a colleague or a glance at a phone returns you to the start. This is the main reason it is so rare in modern office work. People who rely on it protect blocks of time fiercely. They close the door, silence devices and tell others when they will be available again.
Where people find it

Surveys in which people were paged at random moments and asked what they were doing and how they felt produced a surprising result. Flow was reported more often at work than during leisure. Passive leisure, particularly watching television, almost never produced it. Work, for all the complaints about it, has goals, feedback and challenge built in. Leisure produces flow when it is active and skilled, as in sport, music, craft, gardening or games.
What it is not

Flow is not happiness in the ordinary sense. During it, people report feeling very little, because attention is fully occupied. The satisfaction comes afterwards. Nor is it always good for you. Gambling machines and some video games are engineered to produce a flow-like absorption that serves the maker more than the player. And flow does not mean relaxing. It is a state of high effort that happens not to feel like strain.
Arranging it

To make flow more likely, choose a task slightly beyond your comfortable level. Define exactly what done looks like for the next hour. Set up some way to see your progress. Remove every source of interruption you control. Then begin, and tolerate the first quarter of an hour, which usually feels like ordinary effort. You cannot force the state. You can only set the conditions and stay with the work long enough for it to arrive.
The smallest unit

Unit economics means looking at the money a business makes or loses on one unit of what it sells. The unit might be one customer, one order, one ride or one subscription month. The question is simple. After paying the costs that come with that single unit, is anything left over? A company that earns money on each unit can grow its way to covering its fixed costs. One that loses on each unit cannot, however fast it grows.
Contribution margin

Take the price of one unit and subtract the costs that vary with it: materials, packaging, delivery, payment fees, the labour directly involved. What remains is the contribution margin, the amount each sale contributes toward rent, salaries and profit. A meal delivered for 30 dollars that costs 12 in food, 8 in courier pay and 2 in fees contributes 8. If the figure is negative, selling more loses more. The old joke about making it up on volume describes exactly this.
What a customer costs

Customers are not free to obtain. Advertising, sales staff, discounts and free trials all cost money. Add up everything spent on winning customers in a period and divide by the number won, and you have the customer acquisition cost. If a company spends 90,000 dollars on marketing in a month and gains 1,000 customers, each cost 90 dollars. That sum has to be earned back from the customer's purchases before the relationship shows any profit.
What a customer is worth

Lifetime value is the total contribution a typical customer generates before they leave. For a subscription priced at 30 dollars a month with a 60 percent margin, each month contributes 18 dollars. If customers stay 15 months on average, lifetime value is 270 dollars. The length of stay comes from the churn rate, the share of customers who cancel each month. With 5 percent monthly churn, the average customer stays about 20 months.
The ratio

Divide lifetime value by acquisition cost and you get the figure investors ask about first. In the example, 270 divided by 90 is 3. A ratio of about 3 to 1 is a commonly quoted rule of thumb for a healthy business. A ratio near 1 means the company is merely swapping marketing dollars for revenue dollars. A very high ratio can mean the company is underinvesting in growth. The exact target varies by industry, and the direction over time matters most.
Payback time

A good ratio is not enough if the money takes too long to return. The payback period is how many months of contribution it takes to recover the acquisition cost. Ninety dollars recovered at 18 dollars a month takes five months. During that time the company is out of pocket for every new customer, so faster growth needs more cash. Many subscription businesses aim to recover the cost within a year. Longer than that and growth must be funded by investors or debt.
Where the estimates go wrong

Every input is an estimate, and the errors usually flatter. Lifetime value assumes customers will stay as long as earlier ones did, though customers won by heavy discounting tend to leave sooner. Acquisition cost often omits salaries and counts customers who would have arrived anyway. Early customers are the easiest to win, so cost per customer generally rises as a company grows. Careful analysis tracks each month's new customers as a separate group to see how they really behave.
Using it yourself

The same thinking applies to a market stall or a freelance practice. Work out what one sale truly contributes after its direct costs. Work out what you spend, in money and time, to win one customer. Estimate how much a customer brings in over the whole relationship. If the numbers do not work for one customer on paper, they will not work for a thousand. If they do, you know how much you can afford to spend to find the next one.
A forced discount

The big blind is the only seat that enters every hand with money already in the pot. When someone raises, you are not paying the full price to continue. You are paying the difference. Against a raise to two and a half big blinds from the button, with the small blind folding, there are four big blinds in the pot and it costs you one and a half more. You are getting better than 2.5 to 1, and you close the action, so nobody can raise behind you.
The raw number

At that price you need only about 27 percent equity to break even on the call, if the hand simply ran to showdown. Against a minimum raise to two big blinds, the requirement drops to about 22 percent. Almost any two cards have that much against a wide button range. Seven two offsuit has roughly 30 percent against a typical late position opener. If raw equity were the whole story, you would defend almost everything.
Why you cannot defend everything

The whole story includes what happens after the flop. You will be out of position on every street, acting first with less information. Weak hands frequently win less than their share of the pot in that spot. They are forced to fold to bets when they would have won, and they pay off when they make a second-best pair. This shortfall is called failing to realize equity, and offsuit, disconnected hands suffer from it most.
Hands that play well

The hands that defend best are those that can make strong holdings or strong draws. Suited cards realize their equity far better than offsuit ones, because they can continue on more flops. Connected cards make straights. Pairs can flop sets. So queen six suited is a reasonable call against a button raise, while queen six offsuit is close to a fold. The two hands differ by only a few points of raw equity and by a great deal in practice.
Size and position of the raiser

Your defending range should stretch and shrink with the situation. Against a small raise, defend wide. Against a raise to four big blinds, the price is much worse and you should tighten considerably. The raiser's seat matters as much. A raise from under the gun represents a strong, narrow range and deserves respect. A raise from the button could be nearly half of all hands, and folding too much against it lets that player profit with any two cards.
Reraising from the blind

Calling is not the only way to defend. Reraising with your strongest hands builds a pot when you are ahead, and mixing in some bluffs with hands such as suited aces and suited kings punishes players who open too widely. Because you will be out of position, make these reraises large, around four times the opening raise. A blind that only ever calls is easy to play against. One that sometimes comes back over the top makes late position raisers think twice.
With antes in play

In tournaments, every player or the big blind alone often posts an ante on top of the blinds. That extra money in the middle improves the price further. Facing a small raise with antes in the pot, the big blind may need less than 20 percent equity, and the correct defending range becomes very wide indeed. Players who learned in games without antes routinely fold far too much from the big blind in tournaments and bleed chips each orbit.
After you defend

Defending widely only works if you play sensibly afterwards. Most of the time you will miss the flop and should simply check and fold to a bet. When you connect, lean toward checking and raising your strong hands and good draws instead of leading out. Do not pay off three streets with a weak top pair against a tight opponent. The aim from the big blind is modest: lose less than the one big blind that folding every time would cost.
Arrival

In October 1347, trading ships from the Black Sea put in at Messina in Sicily with dead and dying sailors aboard. The disease they carried had been moving west across Asia for years along the caravan routes. From Sicily it spread through the ports of the Mediterranean and then inland along roads and rivers. By 1348 it had reached Paris and London. By 1350 it was in Scandinavia. Within about four years it had passed through almost every part of Europe.
The disease

The cause was a bacterium, Yersinia pestis, carried by fleas that live on rats and other rodents. Bitten people developed fever and painful swellings in the groin, armpit or neck, called buboes, which gave bubonic plague its name. Around half of those infected died, usually within a week. When the infection reached the lungs, it spread directly from person to person through coughing, and that form was almost always fatal. DNA recovered from medieval plague burials has confirmed the identification.
The scale

Nobody counted the dead precisely, but historians estimate that Europe lost between a third and a half of its population in those few years, tens of millions of people. Some towns and villages were emptied entirely. Florence may have lost more than half its inhabitants. Monasteries, where people lived close together, were devastated. There were too few living to bury the dead properly, and mass graves were dug outside city walls.
How people understood it

With no knowledge of germs, people looked for other explanations. Physicians blamed corrupted air or an unfavourable alignment of the planets. Many saw divine punishment, and processions of penitents whipped themselves through the streets. Others looked for someone to blame. Jewish communities were accused of poisoning wells and were massacred in many towns across the Rhineland and beyond, despite a papal statement that the accusation was false.
Quarantine

Some responses did help. Italian ports began to isolate arriving ships and travellers before allowing them ashore. The city of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, introduced a thirty-day isolation period in 1377, and Venice later extended it to forty days. The Italian for forty days gave us the word quarantine. Officials did not know why isolation worked. They had observed that it did, and public health boards with real powers were among the lasting institutions the plague produced.
Labour becomes scarce

The economic effects were profound. With so many dead, workers were suddenly in short supply and land was plentiful. Surviving peasants and labourers could demand higher wages and better terms, or leave for a lord who offered more. Authorities tried to stop this. England passed a law in 1351 to hold wages at their earlier level. It was widely evaded, and resentment of such measures fed the great English peasant revolt of 1381.
Longer consequences

Historians continue to argue over how far the plague altered the course of European history. Many hold that higher wages and scarce labour weakened serfdom in western Europe and encouraged labour-saving methods. The shock to the Church's authority, when prayer and clergy proved powerless, may have prepared ground for later religious upheaval. What is certain is that the population of Europe took roughly a century and a half or more to recover its earlier level.
It came back

The Black Death was the worst wave of a pandemic that kept returning. Outbreaks struck somewhere in Europe every few years for the next three centuries, including the Great Plague of London in 1665. The disease still exists in wild rodent populations on several continents and causes a small number of human cases each year. Today it is treated with common antibiotics, and when treated promptly it is rarely fatal.
A very high gain amplifier

An op-amp has two inputs, marked plus and minus, and one output. It amplifies the difference between the inputs by an enormous factor, typically 100,000 or more. On its own that is nearly useless, because the tiniest difference slams the output against one supply rail or the other. The cleverness lies in feeding part of the output back to the minus input. This is called negative feedback, and it tames the huge gain into something precise and predictable.
The two golden rules

With negative feedback in place, two rules describe what happens. First, the inputs draw no current. Second, the output does whatever it must to make the voltages at the two inputs equal. Neither is exactly true, but both are close enough for nearly all design work. With those two statements and Ohm's law, you can work out the behaviour of amplifiers, filters, adders and many other circuits without knowing anything about the transistors inside the chip.
The follower

The simplest circuit connects the output straight back to the minus input and puts the signal on the plus input. By the second rule, the output must equal the input. That sounds pointless, but it is very useful. The input draws no current, so it does not disturb a delicate source such as a sensor, while the output can drive a load. This arrangement is called a buffer or voltage follower. It solves the loading problem that spoils a plain voltage divider.
Setting gain with two resistors

Add a pair of resistors and you get amplification. In the non-inverting amplifier, a divider feeds a fraction of the output back to the minus input, and the gain is one plus the ratio of the two resistors. A 9 kilohm and a 1 kilohm resistor give a gain of exactly ten. In the inverting amplifier, the gain is simply the ratio of the feedback resistor to the input resistor, with the signal flipped. The chip's own enormous gain drops out of the result.
Limits you will meet

Real op-amps have boundaries. The output cannot swing beyond the supply voltages, and with many parts it stops a volt or two short of them. Types described as rail to rail come much closer. Speed is limited too. A figure called the gain bandwidth product says how much gain is available at a given frequency. A part rated at 1 megahertz can provide a gain of 100 only up to about 10 kilohertz. Ask for more and the output lags and distorts.
The comparator

Without feedback, an op-amp simply compares its inputs. If the plus input is higher, the output goes to the positive rail. If lower, to the negative. That is a comparator, useful for detecting when a voltage crosses a threshold, such as a battery falling below a safe level or a room getting dark. Dedicated comparator chips do the job faster and more cleanly, but an ordinary op-amp will serve at low speeds.
Classic parts

A handful of op-amps have been in production for decades. The 741, introduced by Fairchild in 1968, is the textbook example and is still sold. The LM358 contains two amplifiers, runs from a single supply and costs a few cents. The TL072 is a low-noise favourite in audio equipment. Modern designs offer lower noise, lower power and faster response, but the pin layout of the common eight-pin dual op-amp has barely changed, so newer parts usually drop into old sockets.
Where they turn up

Op-amps condition the tiny signals from sensors before a microcontroller measures them. They are the heart of audio mixers, guitar pedals and equalizers. They form active filters that select or reject ranges of frequency. They regulate, integrate, add and subtract. The name comes from their original job in analog computers of the 1940s, performing mathematical operations on voltages. If you open almost any device with a microphone or a sensor, you will find at least one.
The main shutoff

Every house has a valve that stops all water entering it. It is usually found where the supply pipe comes through the foundation or floor, often in a basement, crawl space, utility room or garage, and commonly near the water meter. In warm climates it may be outside on an exterior wall. There is often a second valve at the meter by the street, which belongs to the water company. Find yours now, while nothing is leaking.
Two kinds of valve

Older houses tend to have gate valves, which have a round handle like a garden tap and take several full turns clockwise to close. Newer ones have ball valves, with a straight lever. A ball valve is open when the lever lies along the pipe and closed when it is turned a quarter turn to sit across it. Gate valves that have not been touched in years can stick or fail to close fully.
Test it

Once a year, close the main valve and open a tap to confirm that the flow stops. A valve that is stuck, or one that lets water continue to trickle, should be replaced by a plumber before you need it. Do not force a seized gate valve, since the stem can snap. Hang a tag on the valve so that anyone in the household, or a neighbour looking after the house, can identify it quickly.
Fixture valves

Most sinks and toilets have their own small shutoff valves on the pipes beneath them, and washing machines have a pair behind them. These let you isolate one fixture without cutting water to the whole house. If a toilet is overflowing or a tap connector is spraying, turn the small valve under it clockwise until it stops. These valves also seize with age, and they are worth turning off and on once in a while.
If a pipe bursts

The order of action matters. Shut off the main valve first. Then open the lowest cold tap in the house to drain what remains in the pipes, and turn off the water heater so that it does not run dry while heating. If water is near electrical outlets or appliances, switch off the affected circuits at the panel before stepping into it. Then move belongings, photograph the damage for insurance and call a plumber.
Frozen pipes

Water expands when it freezes and can split a pipe. The split often goes unnoticed until the thaw, when the leak begins. Pipes in unheated spaces and outside walls are most at risk. In a severe cold spell, let vulnerable taps drip slightly, open cupboard doors under sinks to let warm air in and keep the heating on if you are away. Garden taps should be shut off from inside and drained before winter.
The silent leaks

Not all leaks are dramatic. A toilet that runs between flushes can waste a great deal of water in a month. Put a few drops of food colouring in the cistern and wait fifteen minutes without flushing. If colour appears in the bowl, the rubber flapper valve is leaking, and replacing it is a cheap, simple job. To check the whole house, turn off every tap and watch the meter. If it is still moving, water is escaping somewhere.
Going away

For any absence longer than a few days, consider closing the main valve before you leave. A failed washing machine hose or a leaking connector in an empty house can run for a week. With the water off, the worst case is whatever was already in the pipes. Some homeowners fit leak sensors or automatic shutoff valves that close the supply when water is detected on the floor, which insurers increasingly encourage.
An old experiment

In 1908 two psychologists, Robert Yerkes and John Dodson, trained mice to choose between two boxes, using mild electric shocks as the incentive. Stronger shocks made the mice learn faster, up to a point. Beyond that point, learning got worse. When the task was made harder, the best shock level was lower. Their finding, generalized to humans and to arousal of all kinds, became one of the most cited ideas in psychology, though the original evidence was thin.
The inverted U

The usual picture is a curve shaped like a hill. On the left, at low arousal, you are sleepy, bored and unfocused, and performance is poor. As arousal rises, attention sharpens and energy increases. At the top is a zone of best performance. Beyond it, on the right, lie anxiety, tunnel vision and mistakes. The same racing heart that helped you at a moderate level now gets in the way of thinking clearly.
Simple and complex tasks

The peak sits in a different place for different tasks. Simple, well-practised or physical tasks tolerate high arousal and may even benefit from it. A sprinter or a weightlifter wants to be highly activated. Tasks that need fine judgement, working memory or creativity are disrupted much sooner. A surgeon, a chess player or someone taking an examination does best when alert but calm. Getting psyched up helps the first kind of task and harms the second.
Why too much hurts

Under strong stress, the body prepares for physical action. Stress hormones rise, attention narrows to the perceived threat and the brain regions that support planning and flexible thinking become less effective. That is useful when escaping danger and useless when solving a problem. People under heavy pressure fall back on habit, miss information at the edges and find that their minds go blank. Skills that are deeply practised survive best, which is why emergency crews train to the point of automatism.
Choking

Experts sometimes fail under pressure at things they can do perfectly well in practice. One explanation is that anxiety makes them attend consciously to movements that normally run automatically, and conscious control is slower and clumsier. A golfer who thinks about the mechanics of the putting stroke putts worse. Routines help, because they occupy attention with something harmless. So does practising under realistic pressure, so that the feeling becomes familiar.
How you read the feeling

The physical signs of anxiety and excitement are nearly identical: fast pulse, quick breathing, butterflies. Some experiments have found that people who tell themselves they are excited before a performance do better than those who try to calm down, since moving from anxious to excited is a smaller step than moving to calm. Results in this area are not all consistent, but the technique costs nothing. Treating the symptoms as readiness, not as a warning, is worth trying.
Moving along the curve

You can shift your position deliberately. If you are too far to the right, slow your breathing with long exhalations, which engages the body's calming response within a minute or two. Narrow your focus to the next small step. If you are too far to the left, on a dull afternoon, raise arousal: move about, play music, add a deadline or a small stake, or work near other people. The skill is noticing which side of the hill you are on.
Short stress and long stress

The curve describes pressure in the moment. Stress that continues for weeks or months is a different matter. It impairs sleep, memory and mood, and offers no benefit to performance. Brief demands followed by recovery make people more capable, much as exercise does. Unrelieved demand without recovery wears them down. A period of intense effort is sustainable only if there is a real break at the end of it.
Why price matters so much

Consider a company with sales of 100 dollars, costs of 90 and a profit of 10. If it raises prices by 1 percent and sells the same quantity, sales become 101 and costs stay at 90. Profit rises to 11, an increase of 10 percent. No other change of 1 percent has that effect. Selling 1 percent more units brings extra costs with it. Because price increases fall straight to the bottom line, price is the most powerful lever in most businesses.
Cost-plus

The commonest method is to add up costs and apply a markup. A product that costs 20 dollars to make is sold for 30. It is simple, and it guarantees a margin on each sale. Its weakness is that it ignores the customer entirely. The buyer neither knows nor cares what the product cost to make. Cost-plus pricing charges too little when the product is highly valued and too much when it is not. Cost is a floor, not a guide.
What competitors charge

A second method is to look at rivals and price near them. This keeps a business in line with the market and is sensible for goods that buyers see as interchangeable. The risk is that everyone copies everyone else, and nobody has worked out what the product is actually worth. Matching a competitor's price also means inheriting their mistakes. A company with a genuinely better product that prices at the market rate is giving the difference away.
Value to the customer

The third approach starts from the customer. What is this worth to the buyer, compared with their next best alternative? A tool that saves a tradesperson five hours a week is worth far more than the metal in it. Value-based pricing sets the price as a share of that benefit. It requires understanding customers well, which is harder than adding up costs. Businesses that do it tend to earn more, and their customers still come out ahead.
Different buyers, different prices

Customers differ in what they are willing to pay. A single price loses money at both ends: some would have paid more, and some who would have paid less buy nothing. Businesses respond with versions. Airlines sell the same journey at several prices with different conditions. Software comes in basic, standard and premium tiers. Cinemas discount for students and matinees. Offering a few distinct options lets each buyer choose the price that suits them.
The power of three options

When shown three tiers, many buyers avoid the cheapest and the dearest and choose the middle. Sellers use this deliberately. A premium option priced very high makes the middle one look moderate, even if few people buy the premium. The top tier earns its place by changing how the others are perceived. If you sell a service, offering three clearly different packages often raises the average sale without changing any single price.
The psychology of the number

Details of presentation shift behaviour. A price of 19.99 is read as noticeably cheaper than 20, because people give most weight to the first digit. A price shown next to a higher crossed-out figure appears to be a bargain. A monthly figure looks smaller than the same amount stated annually. None of this changes what the buyer pays. All of it changes how the price feels, and sellers are well aware of the effects.
Raising prices

Most small businesses charge too little and fear that any increase will drive customers away. The arithmetic is worth doing. A firm with a 30 percent margin that raises prices by 10 percent can lose a quarter of its customers and still make the same profit, while doing less work. In practice, far fewer usually leave. The sensible approach is to test: raise the price for new customers first, watch what happens, and adjust.
The ratio

Stack-to-pot ratio, usually shortened to SPR, is the smaller of the two players' remaining stacks divided by the size of the pot when the flop is dealt. If the pot holds 20 dollars and each of you has 200 behind, the SPR is 10. If the pot holds 60 and you each have 180, it is 3. The figure describes how much betting is still possible relative to what is already in the middle, and that governs how hands should be played.
Where typical values come from

Suppose stacks are 100 big blinds. A raise to 3 and one call from the button, with the blinds folding, makes a pot of 7.5 big blinds with 97 behind, an SPR of about 13. Now suppose there is a reraise to 10 and a call. The pot is about 21 and the stacks 90, an SPR a little above 4. The reraise did not just make the pot bigger. It changed the kind of hand that is being played.
Low ratios favour one pair

When the SPR is around 4 or lower, one or two bets will put the remaining money in. Hands such as an overpair or top pair with a good kicker are strong enough to commit with, because opponents will put their stacks in with worse pairs and draws. There is little room for an opponent to outplay you on later streets. In low SPR pots, the decision is largely made on the flop: either the hand is good enough to go with or it is not.
High ratios demand more

When the SPR is 10 or more, there are three full streets of betting ahead. If all of that money goes in, the winning hand is rarely one pair. It is two pair, a set, a straight or a flush. Top pair becomes a hand to win a medium pot with, not to stack off with. Many players lose their biggest pots by treating an overpair in a deep pot as though it were the nuts.
Speculative hands need depth

The same logic explains which starting hands gain or lose value. Small pairs and suited connectors are trying to make hidden, powerful hands and win a big pot. They need a high SPR to be paid enough when they hit. Big unpaired cards such as ace king prefer a low SPR, because their usual made hand is top pair, and top pair is happiest when the money goes in early.
You can shape it

SPR is not something that merely happens to you. Your sizing before the flop sets it. Raising larger or reraising lowers it, which suits big pairs and big cards. Keeping the pot small with a call preserves a high SPR, which suits speculative hands in position. Good players think one step ahead: with this hand against this opponent, what kind of pot do I want to be playing after the flop?
Commitment

A useful question on the flop is whether you are committed, meaning willing to put the rest of your stack in. With a low SPR and a strong pair, the answer is usually yes, and you should play to get the money in. With a high SPR and the same pair, the answer is no, and you should aim to control the size of the pot, often by checking one street. Deciding this early prevents the worst outcome: betting twice and then folding.
A habit for every flop

Before acting on any flop, glance at the pot and the shorter stack and estimate the ratio. Under 4, play strong pairs fast. Between 4 and 10, proceed with care and let the board and the opponent guide you. Above 10, remember that big pots belong to big hands. The estimate takes a second. It prevents overplaying one pair when deep, and it prevents folding the best hand when the pot is already too large to give up.
What actually ended

The traditional date is the year 476, when a general named Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, a boy called Romulus Augustulus, and did not bother to replace him. By then the western empire controlled little beyond Italy. Importantly, only half of the empire ended. The eastern half, governed from Constantinople, continued for nearly a thousand years more, until the city fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453. Its people called themselves Romans to the end.
A century of crisis

The trouble began much earlier. In the third century the empire nearly disintegrated. In about fifty years there were more than twenty emperors, most of whom died violently. Armies fought each other to install their own generals. Plagues killed large numbers. The government paid its soldiers by reducing the silver in the coinage until it was nearly worthless, producing severe inflation. The empire survived, but as a more militarized, heavily taxed and rigid state.
An empire too large for one ruler

At the end of that century, the emperor Diocletian concluded that the empire was too big for one man to defend and divided its administration between east and west. Constantine later founded a new capital in the east, in 330, on the site that became Constantinople. The eastern half was richer, more urban and easier to defend. Over time, the two halves grew apart, and the west, with longer frontiers and less money, became the weaker partner.
Pressure on the frontiers

In the late fourth century, the Huns moved into eastern Europe from the steppe and pushed other peoples before them. Large groups of Goths sought refuge inside the empire. Mistreated by Roman officials, they rebelled, and in 378 they destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople and killed the eastern emperor. From then on, whole peoples under their own kings lived inside the frontiers, sometimes as allies and sometimes as enemies.
The army changes

Rome increasingly relied on these groups to do its fighting, settling them on land in return for military service. This was cheaper than raising and training Roman recruits, and it worked for a time. But such forces were loyal to their own leaders first. In 410 a Gothic army under Alaric, which had served Rome and felt cheated of its rewards, sacked the city of Rome itself. The shock was felt across the Mediterranean world.
Losing the tax base

The decisive losses were financial. As provinces passed under the control of Goths, Franks, Vandals and others, their taxes stopped reaching the imperial government. The gravest blow came in 439, when the Vandals seized North Africa, the richest region of the west and the main source of grain for the city of Rome. With less revenue, the state could pay fewer soldiers, and with fewer soldiers it lost more territory. The spiral did not reverse.
The argument about causes

In the eighteenth century, the English historian Edward Gibbon wrote the most famous account and gave much of the blame to the loss of civic virtue and the rise of Christianity. Few historians now accept that. A German scholar once catalogued 210 different causes that had been proposed. Current explanations emphasize the combination of civil war, fiscal weakness and external pressure. Some historians stress violent collapse. Others see a gradual transformation into the kingdoms of early medieval Europe.
What was lost and what survived

In the west, the changes were real. Cities shrank dramatically, and the population of Rome itself fell from perhaps a million to a few tens of thousands. Long-distance trade declined, and literacy became rarer. Yet much endured. Roman law, the Latin language and the Christian Church carried on, and the new kings governed with Roman officials and titles. French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian are all Latin, spoken continuously and changed over time.
What it measures

A digital multimeter measures the three basic quantities: voltage, current and resistance. Most also check continuity with a beep and test diodes, and many add capacitance, frequency or temperature. A perfectly serviceable one costs about the price of a restaurant meal. The black lead goes in the socket marked COM and stays there. The red lead goes in the socket marked for volts and ohms for almost everything you will do.
Voltage: across the part

To measure voltage, set the dial to volts, DC or AC as appropriate, and touch the probes to the two points you want to compare. The meter sits in parallel with the circuit, which stays powered and undisturbed. For most work, clip the black lead to ground and probe with the red. Because a meter in this mode has a very high resistance, typically 10 megohms, it draws almost nothing and rarely affects the circuit being measured.
Resistance: power off

To measure resistance, set the dial to ohms and touch the probes to each end of the part. The meter passes a small current of its own through the part and measures the result. This only works if the circuit is unpowered. Other parts connected in parallel will lower the reading, so for an accurate value, disconnect one end of the component first. Touching the probe tips together should read close to zero, which checks your leads.
Continuity: the beep

The continuity setting sounds a tone when the resistance between the probes is very low. It is the fastest way to answer everyday questions. Is this wire broken? Are these two pins connected? Has this fuse blown? Is this switch working? Because you can listen instead of looking at the display, you can keep your eyes on the probes. Like resistance, it must be used with the power off. Many experienced technicians use this function more than any other.
Current: through the meter

Current is the awkward one. The meter must become part of the circuit, so you break the path and connect the probes across the gap, making the current flow through the meter. You must also move the red lead to the socket marked for amps or milliamps. Start on the higher current range if you are unsure. For many jobs it is easier to measure the voltage across a known resistor and calculate the current with Ohm's law.
The classic mistake

In current mode the meter is nearly a dead short between its probes. If you leave the red lead in the amps socket and then try to measure a voltage, you place that short across the supply. On a small battery this blows the meter's internal fuse. On a car battery or mains it can be violent. Make a habit of returning the red lead to the volts socket as soon as you finish any current measurement.
Safety ratings

Meters carry a category rating printed near the sockets, from CAT I to CAT IV, describing the electrical environments they are built to survive. Low-voltage electronics work needs nothing special. Measuring household mains calls for a meter genuinely rated for it, with properly fused inputs and insulated probes, from a reputable maker. Very cheap meters often claim ratings they do not meet. If you are not trained to work on mains wiring, the right setting is not to measure it at all.
Getting the most from it

A few habits make the tool far more useful. Check the meter on a known source, such as a fresh battery, before trusting a surprising reading. Replace its battery when the low-battery symbol appears, since readings drift before the display dims. Buy a set of clip-on probe tips so your hands are free. And remember what the numbers mean. A reading is a clue about the circuit, and the skill lies in knowing what value you expected to see.
What the filter is for

In a forced-air heating and cooling system, a fan pulls air from the rooms, pushes it across a heating or cooling element and sends it back through the ducts. The filter sits in the path of the returning air. Its original and main purpose is to protect the equipment: to keep dust from coating the fan and the coils. Cleaner air for the occupants is a welcome secondary benefit, depending on the grade of filter fitted.
What a clogged filter does

As a filter loads with dust, less air can pass through it. The fan works harder and uses more electricity. In cooling season, reduced airflow lets the cooling coil get too cold, and it can ice over and stop working. In heating season, the furnace runs too hot and a safety switch shuts it down. Many service calls for a system that has stopped heating or cooling end with the technician pulling out a filter that is grey and matted.
The rating scale

Filters are graded on a scale called MERV, which for household products runs from about 1 to 16. Higher numbers capture smaller particles. Cheap fibreglass filters, rated around 1 to 4, stop lint and little else. Pleated filters rated about 8 catch most dust, pollen and mould spores and suit the majority of homes. Filters rated 11 to 13 capture finer particles, including much of the smoke from wildfires, and are favoured by people with allergies.
Higher is not always better

A denser filter resists airflow more. Some systems, especially older ones with the common one-inch filter slot, were not designed for a high-rated filter and can suffer the same problems as with a clogged one. If you want finer filtration, check the equipment's manual or ask a technician. Systems built with a thicker filter cabinet, taking a filter four or five inches deep, handle high ratings easily, because the larger surface area offsets the resistance.
How often

For a standard one-inch pleated filter, check monthly and expect to replace it every one to three months. Homes with pets, smokers, construction dust nearby or heavy use need the shorter interval. Thicker filters last six months to a year. The simplest test is to hold the filter up to a light. If you cannot see light through it, replace it. Setting a recurring reminder on your phone works better than relying on memory.
Changing it

Turn the system off at the thermostat. Find the filter, which sits either behind a return air grille in a wall or ceiling or in a slot beside the furnace or air handler. Slide the old one out and note the size printed on its frame. Slide the new one in with the arrow on its frame pointing in the direction the air travels, toward the fan. Fitting it backwards makes it less effective and can cause it to collapse.
The savings

The United States Department of Energy estimates that replacing a dirty filter with a clean one can lower an air conditioner's energy use by 5 to 15 percent. The larger saving is in avoided repairs and longer equipment life, since strained fans and overheating furnaces fail early. Buying filters in multi-packs and writing the installation date on the frame with a marker makes the habit easy to keep.
The rest of the system

While you are there, a few other checks help. Keep supply and return vents clear of furniture and rugs. Keep the outdoor unit of an air conditioner free of leaves and with clear space around it. Have the system inspected by a technician every year or two. Any fuel-burning furnace should be accompanied by working carbon monoxide alarms in the home, tested regularly, since the gas has no smell and can be fatal.
Years are not enough

Many people do a job for twenty years without improving after the first two. Studies have found that some doctors, for example, are no more accurate at certain diagnoses late in their careers than early on. Once a skill is good enough to get by, it becomes automatic, and automatic performance stops developing. Repetition maintains a level. It does not raise it. The question that interested the psychologist Anders Ericsson was what the people who keep improving do differently.
The violinists

In a well-known study published in 1993, Ericsson and colleagues examined violin students at a music academy in Berlin. The students judged most likely to become international soloists had accumulated considerably more hours of solitary practice by age twenty than the others, on average around ten thousand. All of the groups spent similar time on music overall. The difference lay in time spent alone, working on specific weaknesses, an activity the students themselves rated as demanding and not much fun.
What makes practice deliberate

Ericsson called this deliberate practice and described its features. It targets a specific aspect of performance just beyond your present ability. It requires full concentration. It provides immediate feedback on what went wrong. It involves repeating the difficult part, with corrections, until it improves. And it is usually designed by a teacher or coach who knows how the skill is built. Playing a whole piece through for pleasure meets none of these conditions.
The edge of ability

The essential ingredient is working at the boundary of what you can do. Below that boundary, practice is comfortable and teaches little. Far above it, you flounder. At the edge, you fail often, and each failure carries information. This is why deliberate practice is tiring. Even elite performers in Ericsson's studies could manage only about four hours a day of it, usually in sessions of an hour or so, and many took naps.
Feedback

Without knowing what you did wrong, repetition merely fixes your mistakes in place. Good practice builds in a fast and honest signal. A coach watching. A recording you listen back to. A chess engine that shows the better move. A written answer checked against a model solution. Fields with rapid, clear feedback, such as chess and music, produce reliable expertise. Fields where feedback is slow or ambiguous, such as long-range forecasting, often do not.
The ten thousand hour myth

The figure became famous through popular books, in a form Ericsson himself objected to. Ten thousand hours was an average for one group of violinists at age twenty, not a threshold, and individuals varied widely. Hours of the wrong kind count for little. And practice is not the whole story. A 2014 analysis combining many studies found that deliberate practice accounted for roughly a quarter of the differences in skill in games and a fifth in music, and much less in other fields.
What else matters

The remaining differences reflect things such as starting age, physical and mental aptitudes, the quality of teaching and opportunity. Height matters in basketball however hard one trains. This does not make practice unimportant. It remains the largest factor that an individual controls, and nobody reaches a high level without a great deal of it. It simply means that effort is necessary and does not guarantee the same result for everyone.
Applying it

For any skill you want to improve, identify the specific component that is holding you back. Design an exercise that isolates it. Find a source of immediate feedback. Work on it in short, concentrated sessions, and stop when concentration fades. Then repeat on another day. A cook might practise only knife cuts for twenty minutes. A writer might rewrite one paragraph five ways. An hour of this is worth many hours of comfortable repetition.
The problem of success

In an open market, unusual profits do not last. If a coffee shop on a busy corner is making a fortune, another opens across the street. Prices fall, costs rise and returns drift toward ordinary. Economists consider this the normal state of affairs. The interesting cases are the exceptions: companies that earn high returns year after year without being competed down. The investor Warren Buffett popularized the image of a castle protected by a moat to describe them.
Network effects

The strongest moat arises when a product becomes more valuable as more people use it. A payment card is useful because many shops accept it, and shops accept it because many customers carry it. A marketplace attracts buyers because sellers are there, and sellers because buyers are. A newcomer with a better product still starts with an empty network, which is worth little. Such businesses tend toward one or two dominant players and are very hard to dislodge.
Switching costs

A second moat is the trouble customers face in leaving. A company that has run its accounts on one software system for ten years faces retraining, data migration and risk if it changes. A bank customer must move direct debits and salary payments. The product does not have to be the best available. It has to be good enough that switching is not worth the effort. High switching costs allow steady price increases without losing many customers.
Cost advantages

Some companies can simply produce more cheaply than anyone else. Scale is the usual source. A retailer buying in enormous volumes obtains lower prices from suppliers. A manufacturer with the biggest factory spreads its fixed costs over more units. Others own a unique resource, such as a mine with unusually rich ore or a location nobody else can occupy. A low-cost producer can charge prices at which rivals lose money and still make a profit.
Intangible assets

Brands, patents and licences form a fourth category. A patent gives a legal monopoly for a limited period, which is why drug makers earn so much on a medicine until the patent expires. A government licence may limit how many firms can operate. A brand is a moat only if it lets the company charge more or sell more than an identical unbranded product would. Being well known is not enough. Many famous brands have no pricing power at all.
What is not a moat

Several things that look like protection are not. A good product can be copied. Excellent management can leave. Being first to market helps only if it leads to one of the real advantages above. Rapid growth is not a moat, and neither is a large market share won by cutting prices. The test is to ask what would stop a well-funded rival from doing the same thing and taking the customers. If the answer is nothing, there is no moat.
How to spot one

The evidence shows up in the numbers. A company with a durable advantage earns a high return on the capital invested in it, and has done so for many years, through recessions and changes of management. It can raise prices without losing customers. Its market share is stable. New entrants keep failing. One or two good years prove little. A decade or two of consistently high returns suggests that something structural is protecting the business.
Moats drain

No advantage is permanent. Technology shifts can make a moat irrelevant. Film photography was protected by scale and brand, and digital cameras removed the need for film altogether. Patents expire. Regulations change. Customers' habits move. A company with a wide moat can also grow complacent and stop improving. Investors therefore ask not only whether a moat exists but whether it is getting wider or narrower, which is harder to judge and matters more.
Dry boards

A dry flop is one with few possible draws: cards of three different suits that are far apart in rank, such as king, seven, two. On a board like this, hand values are fixed early. Whoever is ahead on the flop will usually still be ahead on the river, because there are few cards that change anything. Bets on dry boards can be small, since there are no draws to charge, and bluffs succeed often, since it is hard for anyone to have connected.
Wet boards

A wet flop is rich in draws: two or three cards of one suit, or cards close together in rank, such as jack, ten, eight with two spades. Many hands have some piece of it, and the best hand now is vulnerable to a large share of the deck. Strong hands should bet larger to make drawing expensive. Bluffing is harder, because opponents have so many reasons to continue. The lead can change on every street.
Paired and monotone boards

Two special cases deserve their own rules. On a paired flop, such as nine, nine, four, it is harder for anyone to hold a strong hand, since only two nines remain. These boards are bluffed at frequently, and small bets work well. On a flop of three cards in one suit, anyone holding a single high card of that suit has a strong draw and anyone without one is in trouble. Play tends to slow down, and big bets from players who lack the suit are risky.
High cards favour the raiser

The player who raised before the flop holds more big cards and big pairs than the player who called. So a flop with an ace or a king generally helps the raiser's overall range more than the caller's. On those boards the raiser can bet frequently, even with nothing, and the caller should be cautious. This idea is called range advantage. It is about who holds the stronger collection of possible hands, not about any one hand.
Low connected cards favour the caller

A flop such as seven, six, five tells the opposite story. A player who called a raise, especially from the big blind, holds many more small pairs, suited connectors and two-pair combinations that hit this board. The raiser's range of big cards has largely missed. Here the raiser should check more often, and the caller can attack. Betting automatically on such a flop because you raised before it is a common and expensive habit.
Who can have the best hands

A related idea is nut advantage: which player can hold the very strongest hands. On a flop of ace, king, four, the preflop raiser can have pocket aces, pocket kings and ace king. The caller would usually have reraised with those and so rarely has them. A player with the nut advantage can bet very large, because the opponent can never be confident. A player without it should keep bets smaller, or check.
Turn and river cards

Texture is not fixed on the flop. A dry board can become wet when the turn brings a second card of a suit and a straight possibility. A third flush card or a fourth card to a straight on the river transforms the value of every hand. Ask of each new card which player it helps. An ace on the turn usually favours the preflop raiser. A low card that completes a straight usually favours the caller.
A quick routine

On every flop, run three questions. How many draws are possible? Whose range does this board hit harder? Who can hold the strongest hands? The answers set your plan before you look at your own two cards. With practice the routine takes a couple of seconds. It also stops the most common beginner error after the flop, which is to think only about what you hold and not about what the board means for both players.
A name invented later

Nobody who used these routes called them the Silk Road. The term was coined in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen. It describes a web of tracks linking China with Central Asia, India, Persia and the Mediterranean, crossing deserts and some of the highest mountain passes on Earth. From the Chinese capital to the eastern Mediterranean was a journey of more than six thousand kilometres. There were also sea routes through the Indian Ocean that carried even more cargo.
How it began

Chinese accounts date regular contact to the second century before the common era. The Han emperor sent an envoy named Zhang Qian westward to seek allies against nomadic raiders. He was captured and held for years, but he eventually returned with reports of rich kingdoms and superb horses in Central Asia. China extended its military reach westward to protect the routes, and trade followed. At the other end, the Roman Empire was developing an appetite for eastern luxuries.
Relay trade

Goods crossed the continent in stages. A bale of silk might change hands a dozen times between China and Syria, each merchant carrying it for one section and selling it on at a profit. Very few individuals travelled the entire distance. Merchants from Sogdiana, the region around Samarkand, dominated the central stretches for centuries. Oasis cities such as Kashgar, Dunhuang and Merv grew rich providing water, lodging, markets and protection to the caravans.
What moved

Silk travelled west and gave the routes their modern name. For centuries only China knew how to make it, and Romans paid for it in gold, to the alarm of some of their writers. Spices, jade, porcelain, lacquer and tea also went west. Glassware, wool, wine, silver and gold went east, along with horses from Central Asia. The trade was in goods light and valuable enough to justify months on the back of a camel.
Ideas travelled further than goods

The most lasting cargo was not for sale. Buddhism spread from India into Central Asia and reached China along these routes. Later, Christianity in its eastern forms and then Islam moved the same way. Technologies crossed too. Papermaking, invented in China, reached the Islamic world in the eighth century and Europe several centuries later. Printing, gunpowder and the magnetic compass followed. Crops, musical instruments, artistic styles and mathematical ideas all moved along the network.
The Mongol century

The routes were at their safest in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, when the Mongol Empire controlled most of the territory between China and eastern Europe. A system of relay stations and guarantees for merchants made long journeys practical. The Venetian Marco Polo travelled to China and back in those years, between 1271 and 1295, and his account astonished European readers. A single political authority across the continent lowered the cost and risk of trade dramatically.
Disease on the caravans

The same connections carried disease. The plague that reached Europe in 1347 is thought to have travelled west along the trade routes from Central Asia in the preceding years. The network that had enriched cities for a millennium delivered the pandemic that killed a large share of their inhabitants. Dense, long-distance links spread whatever enters them, harmful as well as valuable. That observation applies equally to later networks.
Decline

The overland routes faded for several reasons. The Mongol Empire broke up and the roads became more dangerous. In 1498 Portuguese ships reached India by sailing around Africa, opening a sea route that could carry far more cargo at lower cost. Ocean shipping gradually took over long-distance trade between Europe and Asia. The oasis cities declined, and some were abandoned to the sand, where archaeologists rediscovered them in the twentieth century.
What solder is

Solder is a metal alloy that melts at a low temperature and bonds to other metals as it cools, forming an electrical and mechanical connection. The traditional alloy is 63 percent tin and 37 percent lead, which melts at 183 degrees Celsius. Lead-free solder, required in most commercial products, is mostly tin with a little silver and copper and melts closer to 220 degrees. Lead-free is somewhat harder to work with. Beginners practising at home often find leaded solder more forgiving.
Flux does the chemistry

Metal surfaces exposed to air are covered in a thin layer of oxide, and solder will not stick to oxide. Flux is a mild chemical that removes it at soldering temperature and lets the molten metal flow and wet the surface. Electronics solder has flux in its core, which is where the smoke comes from. For surface mount work or reworking old joints, adding extra flux from a pen or syringe makes an enormous difference to how easily the solder flows.
The iron

A temperature-controlled iron is worth the modest extra cost over a plain one. Set it to around 320 to 350 degrees Celsius for leaded solder and a little hotter for lead-free. Keep the tip clean and shiny by wiping it on brass wool and melting a little fresh solder onto it, a step called tinning. A dull, blackened tip transfers heat poorly, and poor heat transfer is behind most beginner frustration. Never file a tip, since the plating is thin.
Heat the joint, not the solder

The technique has one essential rule. Touch the tip of the iron so that it heats both the component lead and the copper pad at once. After a second or so, feed solder into the junction of lead and pad, not onto the iron. The solder should melt against the hot parts and flow around them. Remove the solder, then the iron. The whole operation takes two to four seconds. Longer than that risks lifting the pad or overheating the part.
What good looks like

A good joint on a through-hole board is a small, smooth cone that climbs the lead and spreads across the whole pad, with a slightly concave profile. With leaded solder it is bright and shiny. Lead-free joints are naturally duller, so judge them by shape. A ball perched on the pad means the pad never got hot. A joint that looks grainy or cracked was disturbed while it cooled. Either is called a cold joint, and it may conduct only intermittently.
Fixing mistakes

Too much solder, or a bridge between two neighbouring pins, is easily cured. Desoldering braid is a ribbon of fine copper that soaks up molten solder when pressed onto the joint with the iron. A spring-loaded pump sucks it away. For a bridge between closely spaced pins, adding flux and drawing the clean iron tip along the pins often clears it. Reheating a doubtful joint with a touch of fresh solder, which brings fresh flux, repairs most cold joints.
Safety and habits

The iron will burn skin instantly, so always return it to its stand and never try to catch one that falls. The smoke is vaporized flux, which irritates the lungs, so work with a window open or a small fan drawing it away from your face. Wear glasses, because clipped leads fly and molten solder occasionally spits. If you use leaded solder, wash your hands before eating. Unplug the iron when you leave the bench.
How to practise

Skill at soldering comes quickly with repetition. Buy a cheap practice kit or use a piece of prototype board and a handful of resistors, and make fifty joints in an evening. Inspect each one under good light. Then try removing a few parts cleanly, which teaches as much as attaching them. Within a couple of sessions the timing becomes automatic. After that, surface mount work is the same skill with tweezers, more flux and a steadier hand.
The manual is the authority

Every car comes with a maintenance schedule in the owner's manual, written by the engineers who designed it. It lists what should be inspected or replaced and at what mileage or age. It overrides general advice from friends, forums and service counters. Many cars also calculate oil life and display a reminder. If you have lost the manual, the manufacturer's website normally provides it. Reading the schedule once takes ten minutes and tells you what the car actually needs.
Oil

Oil lubricates and cools the engine and carries away contaminants, and it degrades with use. The old rule of changing it every 3,000 miles dates from an earlier era. Modern engines using synthetic oil commonly go 5,000 to 10,000 miles between changes, as their manuals specify. Check the level with the dipstick once a month, on level ground with the engine off. Running an engine low on oil is one of the few ways to destroy it quickly.
Other fluids

Coolant keeps the engine from overheating and from freezing, and is replaced at long intervals. Brake fluid absorbs moisture from the air over time, which lowers its boiling point and corrodes parts, so many manufacturers call for replacing it every two or three years regardless of mileage. Transmission fluid has its own schedule. Windscreen washer fluid simply needs topping up. Never open the coolant cap on a hot engine, since the system is under pressure.
Filters and belts

The engine air filter keeps dust out of the cylinders and is typically replaced every 15,000 to 30,000 miles, sooner in dusty conditions. The cabin air filter cleans what you breathe. Both are usually easy to change yourself. Engines with a rubber timing belt need it replaced at the interval in the manual, commonly somewhere between 60,000 and 100,000 miles. If it breaks, many engines suffer severe internal damage, so this one should not be postponed.
Brakes

Brake pads wear with every stop. Most have a small metal tab that begins to squeal against the disc when the pad is nearly finished. A grinding noise means the pad material is gone and metal is cutting into the disc, which turns a routine job into an expensive one. A brake pedal that feels soft, sinks or pulses, or a car that pulls to one side under braking, should be inspected promptly.
The battery

A car battery typically lasts three to five years, less in very hot climates. It gives little warning. The usual signs are slow cranking on a cold morning and dimming lights at idle. Many parts shops test batteries without charge. Replacing a battery at four or five years, before it leaves you stranded, is reasonable. Keep the terminals clean and tight. A white or green crust on them can be scrubbed away with a brush.
Warning lights

A steady check engine light means the car's computer has recorded a fault, often minor, and it should be investigated soon. A flashing check engine light indicates an engine misfire that can damage the exhaust system, and calls for easing off and getting the car seen quickly. A red oil pressure or temperature warning means stop as soon as it is safe and switch off. An inexpensive reader plugged into the diagnostic port under the dashboard displays the stored fault codes.
Keep a record

Write down every service with the date and mileage, and keep the receipts. A record tells you what is due, prevents you from paying for the same work twice and adds real value when you sell. It also helps when dealing with a garage. When a service adviser recommends something, compare it with the schedule in the manual. If it is not listed there, ask what specific problem it addresses before agreeing.
First order and beyond

First-order thinking looks at the immediate result of an action. I am hungry, so I eat the cake. Sales are slow, so we cut the price. Second-order thinking asks what happens next, and after that. If we cut the price, competitors will match it, customers will come to expect discounts and the brand will be cheapened. The first-order effect is usually obvious and the same for everyone. Advantage tends to lie in the later effects that most people do not trace.
The rat bounty

In 1902 the French colonial government in Hanoi tried to control a plague of rats by paying a bounty for each rat tail handed in. Tails arrived by the thousand. Then officials noticed rats running about the city without tails. Catchers were cutting off the tails and releasing the animals to breed. Others had begun farming rats. A policy meant to reduce the rat population had created a reason to increase it. A similar story is told about cobras in colonial Delhi.
Incentives change behaviour

The Hanoi episode shows the commonest second-order effect: people respond to the rule, not to its intention. Pay employees per line of code and you get long programs. Judge hospitals on waiting times and patients are kept in ambulances outside. Reward teachers for test scores and they teach to the test. Whenever you set a target or a reward, ask how a clever, self-interested person would meet it with the least effort. Some will do exactly that.
More roads, more traffic

Building a wider road to relieve congestion seems certain to work. Traffic engineers have repeatedly observed otherwise. A faster road makes driving more attractive, so people take trips they would have skipped, travel at peak times instead of off-peak and move further from work. Within a few years the new lanes are as congested as the old. The effect is called induced demand. The first-order reasoning treated the number of drivers as fixed. It was not.
Time and feedback

Later effects are easy to miss because they arrive late and are hard to connect to their cause. An extra hour of work each evening raises output this month. Its effects on health and family appear over years. Antibiotics given freely cure today's infections and breed resistant bacteria over decades. A useful exercise is to ask what the results will be in ten minutes, in ten months and in ten years, and to notice when the answers differ.
How to practise it

The method is a question asked repeatedly: and then what? Write down the decision. Write its immediate effect. For each effect, ask what it will cause and who will react to it. Go two or three steps and stop, since beyond that the chain becomes guesswork. Pay particular attention to how other people will change their behaviour, since ignoring other people's responses is where most first-order reasoning goes wrong.
Good second-order effects

The habit is not only for finding dangers. Many of the best choices are unappealing at first order and excellent afterwards. Exercise is tiring today and strengthening over months. Saving reduces what you can spend now and compounds for decades. Telling a client an unwelcome truth is uncomfortable and builds trust. Learning a difficult skill is slow and then pays for years. Options that look worse at first glance are less crowded, which is part of why they pay.
Humility about prediction

There is a limit. Complex systems cannot be predicted in detail, and confident chains of reasoning about distant effects are frequently wrong. Second-order thinking is not a licence to argue that an obviously beneficial action will secretly backfire. Its sensible use is modest: look a step or two ahead, consider how people will adapt, prefer actions that can be reversed and watch what actually happens so that you can correct course.
The alternative sets your strength

Every negotiation has a shadow: what each side does if the talks fail. A job candidate with another offer in hand negotiates from strength. One with no other prospects does not, however skilled. Negotiation researchers at Harvard gave this a name in the early 1980s: the best alternative to a negotiated agreement, usually shortened to BATNA. It is the course of action you will take if you walk away, and it is the true measure of your position.
Work it out in advance

Before any important negotiation, write down what you will actually do if there is no agreement. Be concrete and realistic. Not that you might find another buyer, but which buyer, at what likely price, after how long. A vague sense that something will turn up is not an alternative. People who skip this step tend either to accept poor deals out of unexamined fear or to reject good ones out of unexamined optimism.
The reservation point

Your alternative determines your walk-away point, the worst terms you should accept. If you have a firm offer of 60,000 dollars elsewhere, taking this job for less makes sense only if it has other advantages you can name. Decide the number before the conversation, when you are calm. During the negotiation, pressure and the wish to reach agreement will push you to shade it. A figure fixed beforehand is an anchor for your own judgement.
The other side has one too

The person across the table also has an alternative and a walk-away point. If a seller will accept anything above 200,000 and a buyer will pay anything up to 230,000, any price in between leaves both better off than no deal. That span is called the zone of possible agreement. If the buyer's limit were below the seller's, no amount of skill would produce a deal, and the sensible outcome would be to part politely.
Estimate theirs

Much of the preparation for a negotiation is working out the other party's alternative. How badly do they need this? What will they do if you leave? How long can they wait? A landlord with an empty flat for three months is in a different position from one with a waiting list. You will rarely know for certain, but an informed estimate tells you how far they can be pushed and guards you against bluffs about other offers.
Improve your alternative

The most effective move often happens away from the table. If your alternative is weak, strengthen it before you negotiate. Get a second quote. Apply for another job. Find another supplier.
