Even a modest second option changes your behaviour, because you no longer need this deal. People negotiating without alternatives give off anxiety, and experienced counterparts notice. Time spent improving your fallback is usually worth more than time spent polishing arguments.
Revealing it

Whether to disclose your alternative depends on its quality. If it is strong, letting the other side know, calmly and without threat, shifts the discussion in your favour. If it is weak, there is no obligation to volunteer it, though you should never lie about it. Inventing a competing offer is risky as well as dishonest. If the other side says to take it, you are left with nothing and a damaged reputation.
Agreement is not the goal

Negotiators often feel that reaching a deal is success and walking away is failure. The right comparison is between the deal on offer and your alternative. If the offer is better, accept it. If not, decline, and do so without resentment. Remembering this protects against the commonest error in bargaining, which is agreeing to something worse than you could have had elsewhere because the conversation had gone on so long.
What it is

A continuation bet, or c-bet, is a bet on the flop by the player who made the last raise before it. The raiser is continuing the story of strength. It works for a simple reason: most hands miss most flops. A player holding two unpaired cards fails to make a pair about two times in three. So whoever bets first often wins, and the preflop raiser, having shown strength already, is the natural candidate to do it.
The price of a small bet

The arithmetic is generous. A bet of one third of the pot needs to succeed only one time in four to break even, even if you never win when called. A bet of half the pot needs one time in three. Against a single opponent who has missed the flop two thirds of the time, that looks like easy money, and for many years players simply bet every flop. Opponents eventually noticed, and automatic c-betting is now a leak that good players exploit.
Best boards for it

C-bets work best on dry flops with high cards, such as ace, eight, three, or king, seven, two. These boards connect with the raiser's range of big cards and miss most of what a caller holds. A small bet, around a third of the pot, with nearly your whole range is a sound play there. Your opponent has to fold most of their hands, and you risk little on the occasions they have something.
Boards to check

On low, connected and suited flops, such as eight, seven, five with two hearts, the caller's range is at least as strong as yours. A bet with nothing will be called or raised a large part of the time. Here it is better to check more of your range, including some reasonably strong hands, so that your checks are not an open invitation to bluff you. Betting should be reserved for strong hands and good draws, usually at a larger size.
Count the opponents

The c-bet is a play for pots with one opponent. Against one player who misses two flops in three, a bluff has a fine chance. Against three players, the chance that all of them missed is small. In pots with several opponents, bet when you have a real hand or a real draw, and check the rest. Firing into a crowd with ace high is one of the fastest ways to lose chips at a loose table.
Position changes the plan

With position, the c-bet is safer. If called, you get to see what your opponent does on the turn before you act. You can also check behind on the flop and take a free card. Out of position, a called c-bet leaves you first to act on the turn with a larger pot and no new information. For that reason, the out-of-position raiser should check more often and be more selective about which hands to bet.
What to bet with

A balanced betting range has three parts. Strong hands that want to build a pot. Draws and hands with a little equity, such as two overcards or a gutshot, which can improve when called. And a few outright bluffs on boards that favour you. Medium hands, such as second pair or a weak top pair, often prefer to check. They are good enough to win at showdown but not strong enough to welcome a raise.
After the flop bet

A c-bet is the first step of a plan, not a single shot. Before betting, decide what you will do on the turn. Good turn cards for a second bet are ones that improve your range or your actual hand: an ace or king, or a card that gives you a draw. If the turn is a blank that changes nothing and you have no equity, checking and giving up is fine. The discipline to stop is what separates a controlled bluff from a spew.
The flat line

Before the eighteenth century, the average person almost everywhere lived at a level not much above subsistence. When harvests improved, populations grew until the gain per person was used up. Economic historians estimate that average income per head changed little for thousands of years. Then output per person in Britain began to rise and kept rising, decade after decade. That sustained growth, more than any single invention, is what the term Industrial Revolution describes.
Cotton

The first transformed industry was textiles. Spinning thread by hand was slow, and a series of machines mechanized it from the 1760s: the spinning jenny, which let one worker spin many threads at once, and the water frame, which used water power to do the same on a larger scale. Weaving was mechanized later. Production moved from cottages to factories built beside rivers. The price of cotton cloth fell sharply, and Britain came to supply much of the world.
Steam

The second ingredient was a new source of power. A crude steam engine had pumped water from mines since 1712. In the 1760s the Scottish instrument maker James Watt redesigned it with a separate chamber to condense the steam, which cut fuel consumption dramatically. Later versions could turn a wheel. Factories no longer needed to stand beside a river. They could be built anywhere coal could be delivered, and they could run in any season.
Coal and iron

Steam needed coal, and Britain had plenty close to the surface and near water transport. Coal also changed ironmaking. Smelting iron had depended on charcoal from dwindling forests. From the early eighteenth century, ironmasters learned to use coke made from coal instead, and iron became cheap and abundant. Cheap iron made better machines, engines, bridges and rails. Each advance fed the others, which is why the changes came as a cluster.
Why Britain

Historians have long debated why it started there. Britain had accessible coal, good waterways and a large trading network. Its wages were high compared with other countries while its energy was cheap, which made machines that saved labour and burned coal unusually profitable. It had secure property rights, an active culture of practical experiment and capital to invest. Most scholars see a combination of these factors, and they disagree about which mattered most.
The human cost

For the first generations of factory workers, the benefits were hard to see. Wages for ordinary workers rose little for decades while output soared. Days of twelve hours or more were standard. Children as young as five or six worked in mills and mines. Cities such as Manchester grew far faster than housing or sanitation, and life expectancy in the poorest districts was shockingly low. Parliament began to restrict child labour in factories in 1833.
Railways

The steam engine put on wheels changed everything again. The first public railway to use steam locomotives opened in the north of England in 1825, and the line between Liverpool and Manchester followed in 1830. Within twenty years Britain had thousands of miles of track. Journeys that had taken days took hours. Fresh food reached cities, coal reached factories, and standard time was introduced across the country so that timetables could work.
The world since

From about the middle of the nineteenth century, wages in Britain began to rise steadily, and the new methods spread to Belgium, Germany, the United States and beyond. The countries that industrialized pulled far ahead of those that did not, creating gaps in wealth that still shape the world. Average incomes in industrial countries are now many times what they were in 1750. The burning of fossil fuels that powered all of it is also the origin of modern climate change.
